blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — systems-based workplace-violence prevention, hazard analysis, reporting, staffing, training, and engineering/security controls
stem: An emergency department has had several incidents involving aggressive visitors, especially when staff work alone in poorly visible hallways. Which prevention strategy best aligns with OSHA guidance?

options.A: Use a prevention program with worksite hazard analysis, visibility/security controls, staff training and reporting, and measures that reduce isolated work.
options.B: Emphasize de-escalation training and post-incident counseling while leaving staffing, visibility, access control, and reporting practices unchanged unless injuries increase.
options.C: Increase cameras and security presence in poorly visible hallways but limit reporting to events that cause injury so resources focus on confirmed workplace assaults.
options.D: Require staff to manage escalating visitors independently before calling security, then review completed assaults to identify individual performance problems.

rationale: A is correct. Current OSHA hospital guidance identifies working alone, understaffing, poor environmental design, inadequate security, lack of staff training/policies, unrestricted public access, and poorly lit areas as workplace-violence risk factors. OSHA recommends a comprehensive Workplace Violence Prevention Program with management commitment, employee participation, worksite analysis, hazard prevention/control, training, recordkeeping and program evaluation. Recognized controls include improved lighting and surveillance, panic/security systems, buddy or escort systems, access controls, de-escalation/reporting training, and adequate staffing. B is incomplete because it leaves key environmental, staffing and reporting hazards unchanged. C adds useful engineering/security controls but incorrectly suppresses reporting of threats and lower-level violent behavior; OSHA encourages prompt reporting and recordkeeping. D is unsafe because working alone is itself a risk factor and OSHA supports security/buddy systems rather than requiring solo management until assault occurs.
educational_objective: Prevent healthcare workplace violence with a comprehensive systems approach that identifies hazards, improves environmental/security controls, trains staff, supports reporting, and reduces avoidable isolated work rather than relying primarily on individual staff behavior.

correction_summary: Original Q0218 had a uniquely longest correct answer and absolute-word distractors. The item was rebuilt with four realistic prevention strategies. The key now tests a comprehensive systems approach; distractors each preserve a partially reasonable intervention but omit or contradict other OSHA-recognized controls.

option_audit.A: Correct; integrates formal program structure, hazard analysis, engineering/security controls, training/reporting, and reduction of isolated work.
option_audit.B: Plausible training-focused plan; incorrect because it leaves recognized staffing, environmental, access-control and reporting hazards unaddressed.
option_audit.C: Plausible engineering/security plan; incorrect because limiting reports to injurious assaults conflicts with OSHA reporting/recordkeeping guidance.
option_audit.D: Plausible autonomy-focused response; incorrect because working alone is a recognized risk factor and security/buddy systems are recognized controls.
